Yes, potentially. Under the policy, an adult with BMI 36 and type 2 diabetes can meet the sleeve gastrectomy criteria, but only if the other requirements below are also documented.

**BMI and comorbidity:** A BMI of 35 to 39.9 kg/m² qualifies when accompanied by at least one listed comorbidity, and "insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes" is one of them [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]. A BMI of 36 with type 2 diabetes meets this part.

**Other criteria:** The policy says sleeve gastrectomy is proven and medically necessary for adults aged 18 or older when all of the following are met [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]:
- One of the BMI options above (here, BMI 35 to 39.9 with type 2 diabetes).
- The individual must also meet both of the following [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]:
  - Completion of a preoperative evaluation that includes a detailed weight history, along with dietary and physical activity patterns; and
  - Either a psychosocial-behavioral evaluation by a professionally recognized behavioral health discipline member, to screen for risk factors or potential postoperative challenges, or participation in a multidisciplinary surgical preparatory regimen.

The policy's Benefit Considerations section is referenced from the coverage rationale, and I did not read it. Please check it for any additional conditions.

For an adult of Asian descent with no other conditions, the policy's threshold is a **BMI of 37.5 kg/m² or greater**. At that level, the person meets the BMI criterion alone. The standard threshold of 40 kg/m² is lowered by 2.5 for Asian descent [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].

Without a qualifying comorbidity, a BMI of 32.5 to 37.4 kg/m² does not meet the criteria. That range qualifies only when one of the listed comorbidities is present, such as insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, or obstructive sleep apnea [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1, p.2].

The policy also requires the following for adults, in addition to the BMI criterion:
- A preoperative evaluation that includes a detailed weight history and dietary and physical activity patterns, and
- Either a psychosocial-behavioral evaluation by a behavioral health professional, or participation in a multidisciplinary surgical preparatory regimen [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].

The Maryland-specific criteria for fully insured group policies use a BMI above 40 without comorbidity, or 35 or greater with comorbidities. They also require a psychological exam and a structured diet program. They do not state an Asian-descent adjustment [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.9].

For an adult with no comorbidities, the threshold is a **BMI of 40 kg/m² or higher** (or 37.5 kg/m² or higher for individuals of Asian descent). No comorbidity is needed at that level. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]

The BMI criterion is one of several that must all be met for adults aged 18 or older. The others are:
- **Age:** The individual must be 18 years or older. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]
- **Preoperative evaluation:** Completion of a preoperative evaluation that includes a detailed weight history, along with dietary and physical activity patterns. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]
- **Psychosocial or multidisciplinary requirement:** A psychosocial-behavioral evaluation by a professional recognized as part of a behavioral health discipline, or participation in a multidisciplinary surgical preparatory regimen. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]

The policy also has a state-specific provision. For fully insured group policies in Maryland only, the criteria follow COMAR: a BMI above 40 kg/m² without comorbidity qualifies, and the adult requirements include a psychological examination and a completed structured diet program. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.9]

No. The UnitedHealthcare Bariatric Surgery policy lists endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty as unproven and not medically necessary for treating obesity, due to insufficient evidence of efficacy. It falls under "Transoral endoscopic surgery, including: Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (includes OverStitch™)" [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3]. The policy also describes the procedure as a minimally invasive, mouth-based technique that uses an endoscopic suturing device such as OverStitch [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.7].

This policy version is effective 2026-05-01, and the 05/01/2026 revision added the transoral endoscopic surgery category wording [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.55].

A planned two-stage bariatric procedure is covered when all three of the following are met:

1. **Initial BMI of ≥ 50 kg/m²** before the first-stage bariatric procedure [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].
2. **Second stage occurs within 2 years** after the primary bariatric surgery [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].
3. **The individual has been adherent to nutrition and exercise** [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]. The 05/01/2026 revision changed this wording from "compliant" to "adherent" [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.55].

The individual must also meet the medical necessity criteria for bariatric surgery at the time of the second-stage procedure [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]. Those general criteria include:

- Age 18 or older, or the separate adolescent criteria for ages 12 to 17 [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1–2].
- A BMI-based indication: Class III obesity, or Class II obesity with one of the listed comorbidities [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1–2].
- Completion of a preoperative evaluation that includes a detailed weight history, dietary and physical activity patterns, and either a psychosocial-behavioral evaluation or participation in a multidisciplinary surgical preparatory regimen [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].

Yes. The policy considers removal of an adjustable gastric band and all related components, when it does not result in a revisional surgery, to be proven and medically necessary [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3]. The policy's code list includes 43772 (removal of the adjustable gastric restrictive device component only) and 43774 (removal of the device and subcutaneous port components) [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.5].

No. UnitedHealthcare's Bariatric Surgery policy lists the intragastric balloon as unproven and not medically necessary for treating obesity, "due to insufficient evidence of efficacy." It appears under "Transoral endoscopic surgery, including: ... Intragastric balloon" in the list of bariatric interventions for obesity [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3].

The policy also notes that the FDA approved the Orbera Intragastric Balloon System for adults with a BMI of 30 to 40 kg/m² who have failed conservative weight-reduction strategies. It states that this FDA information is for informational purposes only and that FDA approval alone is not a basis for coverage [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.43].

No. UnitedHealthcare's Bariatric Surgery policy lists the mini-gastric bypass, also called laparoscopic mini-gastric bypass or one-anastomosis gastric bypass, among the bariatric interventions for obesity that are unproven and not medically necessary due to insufficient evidence of efficacy [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3].

The policy's covered procedures are biliopancreatic diversion with or without duodenal switch, gastric bypass (including robotic-assisted), adjustable gastric banding, and sleeve gastrectomy, when the patient meets the policy's criteria [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].

The minimum age for adjustable gastric banding is 18 years. The policy covers adjustable gastric banding (open or laparoscopic) "for individuals ≥ 18 years of age" [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]. The FDA section also states that adjustable gastric bands are contraindicated in patients younger than 18 years of age [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.44].

Under UnitedHealthcare's Bariatric Surgery policy, a 15-year-old falls under the adolescent rule, which applies to ages 12 to 17. The policy says bariatric surgery is proven and medically necessary for an adolescent when all of the following are met:

1. **Weight criteria (one of):** Class III obesity, or Class II obesity with at least one listed comorbidity. The comorbidities are insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes, poorly controlled hypertension (systolic over 140 or diastolic 90 or higher despite medication), hyperlipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea confirmed on polysomnography with an AHI or RDI of 30 or more, or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].
2. **Multidisciplinary evaluation:** An evaluation at, or in consultation with, a multidisciplinary center focused on surgical treatment of severe childhood obesity. This may include adolescent centers accredited by MBSAQIP or centers that show similar programmatic components [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].

The adolescent rule does not give a specific BMI number. The policy's guidance on adolescent cutoffs appears only in the clinical background, which I cannot treat as UnitedHealthcare's rule.

The policy also has adult criteria, which are not written for adolescents: BMI of 40 or more, or 35 to 39.9 with a comorbidity [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]. Those sections also require a preoperative evaluation with a detailed weight history and dietary and activity patterns, plus either a psychosocial-behavioral evaluation or participation in a multidisciplinary surgical preparation program [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]. The retrieved text does not clearly say whether those requirements also apply to adolescents, so confirm that with UnitedHealthcare or the full policy before relying on it.

Revisional surgery for reflux after a sleeve gastrectomy is covered only when all three of the policy's reflux criteria are met:

1. **Maximum nonpharmacological medical management has failed**, such as positional, dietary modification, or behavioral changes. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]
2. **Maximum pharmacological medical management has failed**, for example at least 1 month of double-dose proton pump inhibitor, H2 blocker, and/or sucralfate. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]
3. **Severe esophagitis (grade C or D) is confirmed by endoscopy** despite maximum medical management. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]

The policy lists this reflux criterion among the technical failures or major complications that qualify for revisional surgery. The sentence introducing that list says the individual must meet the medical necessity criteria at the time of the second-stage procedure. That sentence sits within the planned two-stage procedure section, so the policy's wording does not clearly say whether it applies to a standalone revision. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]

Revisional bariatric surgery for any other indication than the listed complications is unproven and not medically necessary. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3]

The CPT code for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy is **43775** (laparoscopy, surgical, gastric restrictive procedure; longitudinal gastrectomy, i.e., sleeve gastrectomy). The policy's coding clarification says to use 43775 rather than the unlisted laparoscopy code 43659 [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.4], [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.5].

This answers only which code to report. I did not check the coverage criteria for the procedure.

CPT 43889 is a transoral endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG), including argon plasma coagulation when performed. It is listed among the applicable codes in the UnitedHealthcare Bariatric Surgery policy [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.5].

It is not covered for treating obesity. The policy lists "Transoral endoscopic surgery, including: Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (includes OverStitch™)" among the procedures that are unproven and not medically necessary for treating obesity due to insufficient evidence of efficacy [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3]. The policy's description of services explains that ESG uses an endoscopic suturing device to reduce gastric capacity, without removing stomach tissue [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.7].

**Short answer:** For adults, sleep apnea counts as a comorbidity only when it is obstructive sleep apnea confirmed on polysomnography with an Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) or Respiratory Disturbance Index (RDI) of ≥ 30. Milder sleep apnea does not meet this criterion.

**How it applies to adults:**
- Sleep apnea is one of several comorbidities that matter only when BMI is 35 to 39.9 kg/m² (or 32.5 to 37.4 in individuals of Asian descent). A BMI of ≥ 40 kg/m² (or ≥ 37.5 in Asian descent) qualifies without a comorbidity. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]
- The adult comorbidity list includes "Obstructive Sleep Apnea confirmed on polysomnography with an Apnea-Hypopnea Index or Respiratory Disturbance Index of ≥ 30." Other items on the list include history of cardiomyopathy, Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]

**Severity definitions:** The policy defines OSA severity as mild for AHI/RDI ≥ 5 and < 15, moderate for ≥ 15 and ≤ 30, and severe for > 30 per hour. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.4] The coverage criterion uses "≥ 30," while the severity definition labels only values above 30 as severe. The policy text does not reconcile this, so the coverage criterion's "≥ 30" threshold is the one to apply.

**Other adult requirements still apply.** The patient must also complete a preoperative evaluation covering weight history and dietary and physical activity patterns, and complete either a psychosocial-behavioral evaluation or participate in a multidisciplinary surgical preparatory regimen. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]

No. UnitedHealthcare's bariatric surgery policy lists "bariatric surgery as the primary treatment for any condition other than obesity" among the procedures it considers unproven and not medically necessary, due to insufficient evidence of efficacy [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3].

The policy's covered indications are all framed as treating obesity. The proven and medically necessary procedures are described as "for treating obesity" [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]. The policy also notes that most benefit plans exclude coverage for bariatric surgery [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.9], so a member's plan terms also matter.

The clinical evidence sections say there is insufficient evidence for recommending bariatric surgery specifically for glycemic control alone, lipid lowering alone, or cardiovascular disease risk reduction alone [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.35]. These sections are background, not UnitedHealthcare's coverage rule.

The policy defines Class II obesity in adolescents as **120% of the 95th percentile for height, or an absolute BMI of 35 to 39.9 kg/m², whichever is lower**. The definition is attributed to the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery, which also cites the American Heart Association [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3]. The policy text says "height" in the percentile part, although the adolescent classification is normally based on BMI. The policy does not clarify this, so check the wording against the source before relying on it.

For context, the policy's Coverage Rationale allows Class II obesity only with one or more listed comorbidities, such as insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes, poorly controlled hypertension, hyperlipidemia, OSA confirmed on polysomnography with an AHI or RDI of 30 or more, MASLD, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]. The individual must also be evaluated at or in consultation with a multidisciplinary center focused on severe childhood obesity [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].
The UnitedHealthcare bariatric surgery policy is number **2026T0362RR**, with an effective date of **May 1, 2026** [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].

No. Under the UnitedHealthcare Cochlear Implants policy, a non-hybrid cochlear implant for single-sided or asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss is medically necessary only in children ages 9 months or older. A 7-month-old is younger than 9 months, so the policy classes this as experimental or investigational because the device lacks FDA approval for that use [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1].

The policy's coverage for children is also tied to the InterQual CP: Procedures, Cochlear Implantation (Pediatric) criteria, which apply to the covered age groups [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1]. The policy's wording on this point is the same in its OCR copy [uhc-cochlear-implants-scan.pdf p.1].

Non-hybrid cochlear implantation for bilateral sensorineural hearing loss is covered for children **6 months of age or older**. Children younger than 6 months are experimental or investigational because the device lacks FDA approval for that age [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1].

Medical necessity for these children is judged against the InterQual® CP: Procedures, Cochlear Implantation (Pediatric) criteria [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1]. I did not find the InterQual criteria text itself in the policy, so I can't list those clinical conditions here.

Yes, for adults it is covered under certain circumstances. The policy states that hybrid cochlear implantation is "proven and medically necessary under certain circumstances for Sensorineural Hearing Loss in adults ages 18 and older" [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1]. The same statement appears in the companion policy version [uhc-cochlear-implants-scan.pdf p.1].

The policy does not list the specific clinical criteria in the chunks I found. It refers to the InterQual® CP: Procedures, Cochlear Implantation criteria for medical necessity [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1]. To know whether a particular adult patient meets the circumstances, those InterQual criteria would need to be checked.

Coverage for the external components (speech processor, microphone, transmitter coil) falls under the DME benefit, and the implantable components fall under the medical-surgical benefit. The member's benefit plan document determines any DME coverage for repair or replacement of external components [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2]. Post-surgery programming and rehabilitation are usually billed as aural rehabilitation and are covered as an outpatient rehabilitation therapy benefit, subject to any limits in the member's plan [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2].

No. The UnitedHealthcare Cochlear Implants policy excludes FM systems used with cochlear implants. It says FM systems can be used as an extension or accessory of cochlear implants, but they "do not meet the definition of covered health care service and are excluded from coverage." It also says they "do not prevent, diagnose, or treat a sickness or injury, and are not integral to the function of the cochlear implant itself" [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2]. A scanned copy of the same policy says the same thing [uhc-cochlear-implants-scan.pdf p.2].

The policy's code table lists V5273, "Assistive listening device, for use with cochlear implant" [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2]. The table does not say whether that code is covered, and the exclusion above is the only coverage statement I found for FM systems.

The external speech processor falls under the **durable medical equipment (DME) benefit**. The implantable components fall under the medical-surgical benefit. [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2]

The policy also says the member's specific benefit plan document must be checked to see whether DME benefits apply to repair or replacement of external components. [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2]

HCPCS L8619 is "Cochlear implant, external speech processor and controller, integrated system, replacement." [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2]

The OCR'd copy of the same UnitedHealthcare Cochlear Implants policy lists the same description. [uhc-cochlear-implants-scan.pdf p.2]

The CPT code for cochlear device implantation is **69930**, which is described as "Cochlear device implantation, with or without mastoidectomy" [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2]. The same code appears in the scanned copy of the policy [uhc-cochlear-implants-scan.pdf p.2].

This answers only which code describes the procedure. I did not check whether UnitedHealthcare covers the implant. If you need that, I can search the policy's coverage criteria.

Cochlear implant remapping and rehabilitation after surgery are covered under the outpatient rehabilitation therapy benefit. The policy says cochlear implant monitoring (remapping and reprogramming of the implant) and rehabilitation after cochlear implant surgery are usually billed as aural rehabilitation and are covered as an outpatient rehabilitation therapy benefit [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2].

The member's specific benefit plan document must be checked for any limits that apply to aural rehabilitation [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2].
The UnitedHealthcare Cochlear Implants policy is **2026T0070II**, effective June 1, 2026 [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1].

Emergency air ambulance is considered medically necessary only when all of the following criteria are present [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1]:

1. **Need for immediate transport that ground ambulance cannot provide.** The member's condition requires immediate transportation that cannot be provided by ground ambulance, and a delay may endanger the member's life or seriously endanger their health. This includes situations where:
   - ground transport times are excessive (about 30–60 minutes or longer); or
   - weather or traffic makes ground transport impractical, impossible, or overly time-consuming; or
   - the pickup point is inaccessible by ground ambulance and [the policy text is cut off here in the source].
2. **Nearest appropriate destination.** The destination is the nearest acute care hospital that can meet the member's needs.
3. **A qualifying condition during transport.** One of the following exists:
   - services are requested by police or medical authorities at the site of an emergency; or
   - advanced or basic life support is required during transportation.

Air ambulance for any other indication is not considered medically necessary [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1]. Air ambulance transport that doesn't meet these criteria is also excluded, and non-ambulance transport such as a commercial helicopter is not covered even in an emergency [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

The policy doesn't set a fixed number of minutes. It says air ambulance is medically necessary when the member's condition requires immediate transport that ground ambulance cannot provide, and a delay may endanger life or seriously endanger health. One of the examples of that is "when ground transport times are excessive (i.e., 30-60 minutes or longer)" [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1]. The 30 to 60 minute figure is given as an example of excessive transport time, not as a strict cutoff.

Ground transport time is only one route to qualifying. The policy also accepts cases where weather or traffic makes ground transport impractical, impossible, or overly time consuming, or where the pickup point is inaccessible by ground ambulance [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1].

Air ambulance must also meet these conditions [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1]:
- The destination is the nearest acute care hospital that can meet the member's needs.
- Either police or medical authorities requested the service at the scene of an emergency, or advanced or basic life support is required during transport.

The policy states that emergency air ambulance services are not medically necessary for all other indications [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1].

No. Under UnitedHealthcare's ambulance services policy, an Uber, Lyft, or taxi ride to the hospital is not covered, even when the trip is for an emergency. The policy lists "Taxi ride, bus ride, rideshare services such as Lyft and Uber, etc." among non-ambulance transportation that "is not covered even if rendered in an Emergency situation" [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6]. The same exclusion covers a police car ride to a hospital and medi-van or wheelchair van transportation [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

Emergency transportation can be covered when it is provided by a licensed ambulance. Emergency ground ambulance services are considered medically necessary when the member's condition requires immediate transportation to the nearest acute hospital that can provide services appropriate to the illness or injury [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1]. The policy also excludes ambulance transport when another mode of transportation is appropriate, meaning transport by other means would not endanger the member's health [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

Yes. For non-emergency air ambulance transport, the policy states that prior authorization is required [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

Non-emergency ambulance transport is covered between facilities only when it meets one of these conditions, with air or ground transport chosen as UnitedHealthcare determines appropriate:
- From an out-of-network hospital to the closest network hospital when Covered Health Care Services are required.
- To the closest network hospital that provides required Covered Health Care Services that were not available at the original hospital.
- From a Short-Term Acute Care Facility to the closest network Long-Term Acute Care Facility, network inpatient rehabilitation facility, or other network Sub-Acute Facility where the required services can be delivered [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.5].

Air ambulance transport that does not meet the covered indications is not eligible for coverage [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

Yes, in that situation the ambulance service can be covered, but only for emergency ground ambulance services.

- **Emergency ground ambulance services without transport are medically necessary when the ambulance personnel treat the member at the scene.** [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.2]
- **Emergency ground ambulance transportation is not medically necessary for any other indication.** [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.2]
- **Non-emergency treat-and-release is not covered.** The policy's coverage limitations exclude ambulance transportation when other means would be appropriate and the member's health would not be endangered, unless the coverage rationale indicates otherwise. [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6]

The policy also lists a "response and treatment, no transport" code, A0998, and paramedic intercept nontransport codes S0207 and S0208. [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.5] The policy does not state how these codes are reimbursed, so I can't say more about them from these sources.

No. Under the UnitedHealthcare Ambulance Services policy, ambulance transportation to a home is not covered. The policy lists "ambulance transportation to a home, residential, domiciliary, or custodial facility" among services that are not eligible for coverage [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

The policy also lists hospital-to-home transport as "deemed not appropriate" [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6]. Non-ambulance transport, such as taxi, rideshare, or wheelchair van, is not covered even in an emergency [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

Out-of-network emergency ambulance transportation (ground, water, or air) is covered at the network level of deductible and coinsurance, as long as the transport itself is covered [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6]. In other words, the member pays the in-network cost-sharing rather than out-of-network cost-sharing.

"Covered" here also depends on medical necessity. The policy's criteria are:

**Emergency air ambulance** is medically necessary only when all of these are present [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1]:
- The member's condition requires immediate transportation that ground ambulance cannot provide, and a delay may endanger life or seriously endanger health. This includes when ground transport times are excessive (about 30–60 minutes or longer), when weather or traffic makes ground transport impractical or overly time-consuming, or when the pickup point is inaccessible by ground ambulance.
- The destination is the nearest acute care hospital that can meet the member's needs.
- Either police or medical authorities requested it at the site of the emergency, or advanced or basic life support is required during transport.

Air ambulance is not medically necessary for any other indication [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1].

**Emergency ground ambulance** is medically necessary when all of these are present [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1–2]:
- The condition requires immediate transportation to the nearest acute hospital that can treat the illness or injury, to the nearest neonatal special care unit for qualifying newborn conditions, or to a hospital with a required higher level of care not available at the original hospital.
- A delay in transportation may endanger life or seriously endanger health.
- Advanced or basic life support is required during transport.

Emergency ground services without transport are medically necessary when the emergency ground personnel render treatment at the scene. Ground transport that does not meet these criteria is not medically necessary [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.2].

HCPCS A0998 is "Ambulance response and treatment, no transport" [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.5]. It is listed under the Ground/Other Ambulance codes in UnitedHealthcare's Ambulance Services policy (MP.001.25).

QL is the ambulance modifier for "patient pronounced dead after ambulance called." [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.4]

It is an exception to the usual pairing rule. Ambulance claims normally carry two modifiers: the first gives the place of origin and the second gives the destination. The policy states that QL must be billed in place of the origin/destination combination. [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.4]

HCPCS A0431 is "Ambulance service, conventional air services, transport, one way (rotary wing)." It falls under the Air Ambulance codes in the ambulance services policy [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.4].

No. UnitedHealthcare's clinical trials policy excludes the experimental or investigational drug used in the trial, though it covers the routine costs of care around it.

**Excluded:** Benefits for clinical trials do not include the experimental or investigational service or item used in the trial, with a few exceptions [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.3]. The exceptions are:
- **Certain Category B devices.** Only certain FDA-designated Category B devices are covered, and all of these must be met: the device is used within an FDA-approved clinical trial, used according to the trial's approved protocols, falls under a covered benefit category and isn't excluded by law, regulation, or current Medicare coverage guidelines, is medically necessary and used at a medically appropriate amount, duration and frequency, and is furnished in a setting appropriate to the member's needs [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.3].
- **Certain promising interventions for members with terminal illnesses.**
- **Other items and services** that UnitedHealthcare determines meet its specified criteria under its medical and drug policies [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.3].

**Covered:** Routine patient costs are covered for a qualifying member in an approved clinical trial. These are services normally covered absent a trial and required for the delivery of the investigational item (for example, the infusion administration to deliver an investigational drug), for clinically appropriate monitoring, or for preventing complications [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.2]. Benefits also include care for complications arising from trial participation, and they are available only when the member is clinically eligible for the trial as defined by the researcher [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.1]. Lab tests and imaging done only to meet the study protocol's data collection needs are not covered [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.3].

**Other conditions:** For trials treating non-life-threatening conditions, the policy says routine patient costs are not mandated, and coverage depends on the member's specific benefit plan [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.2]. Separately, UnitedHealthcare may consider an otherwise investigational service for a member who is not in a qualifying trial and has a condition likely to cause death within one year, but only after establishing sufficient evidence of significant potential as an effective treatment [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.4].

This answer comes from policy MP.006.27, which lists an effective date of 2026-09-01. Check the member's certificate of coverage for the plan's specific terms.

No. The UnitedHealthcare Clinical Trials policy excludes travel and lodging costs for trial participants. It lists travel and transportation expenses as an exclusion, including lodging (hotel) and meals, and the exclusion covers fares, rental cars, and mileage for a personal vehicle [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.3]. The policy's code table also lists lodging costs (hotel charges) for the participant and one caregiver/companion (S9994) under "Not Covered." Transportation (S9992) and meals (S9996) for the participant and one caregiver/companion are also listed as not covered [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.5].

The policy does cover routine patient costs for a qualifying individual in an approved clinical trial, including services to prevent, diagnose, and treat complications from participation [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.1]. Travel, lodging, and meals are not part of that coverage.

All four phases count: Phase I, Phase II, Phase III, and Phase IV. The trial must also be conducted in relation to the prevention, detection, or treatment of cancer or another life-threatening disease or condition, and it must meet the policy's Criteria for Approved Clinical Trials [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.1].

The policy defines a life-threatening disease or condition as one where the likelihood of death is probable unless the course of the disease is interrupted [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.1].

I did not retrieve the full Criteria for Approved Clinical Trials, so I can't list those requirements here.

No. For an approved clinical trial conducted outside the member's state of residence, UnitedHealthcare may not deny or limit payment for routine patient services solely because the trial is out of state. [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.2]

That protection has conditions and exceptions:

- **Network requirement:** If network providers are participating in the trial, UnitedHealthcare may require the member to participate through a network provider, as long as that provider will accept the member into the trial. [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.2]
